## Asked earlier on this map
- "how does the loop work here at every iteration?": Claude sends back a draft map, and then a loop runs. Each time through, codemap reads Claude's latest reply and checks every claim against the code. It remembers the version with the fewest failed claims. If anything failed, it sends Claude a list of what to correct and goes around again. After at most two correction rounds it stops and keeps the best version, which isn't always the newest one.
- "About “Exploring with follow-ups”:  how does the conversational flow usually work w/ graphs and tooling": A follow-up works like a chat that's tied to the diagram. You click the boxes or arrows you mean, type a question, and Claude answers in the side panel. Its reply can point at parts of the map to highlight them. It can also add new boxes, but only ones that pass the check against the code. Claude tries a quick answer from the map alone first, and only reads the code itself if the map isn't enough. If your question is about a different part of the app, Claude doesn't answer it on this map. It offers to make a new map, or to answer in words only.
- "so does the full conversation thread on every response always follow this flow ?": No. The full flow, where Claude explores the code, the claims get checked, and up to two repair rounds run, happens only when a map is made. After that, each reply in the thread goes through a shorter follow-up path: you ask, Claude answers, and the answer is saved with the map. Each reply can still go one of a few ways. It may be a quick answer from the map alone, or a full answer from reading the code that might add boxes or suggest a fix. If your question is about a different part of the app, Claude offers to make a new map instead. Claude also doesn't see the whole conversation each time, only the last few turns.

## Other maps in this repo
- claude-skill-logic-work-to-start: "How does the Claude skill logic work to start a map? Walk through what happens from the moment a map is requested until Claude has drafted it."
- i-ask-follow-up-question-on: "When I ask a follow-up question on a map, how does Claude decide whether to answer from the map, search the code, or offer a new map, and what happens after each choice?"
- someone-asks-question-on-map-answer: "What happens when someone asks a question on a map: the answer from the map alone, the fallback to searching the code, and how the result gets checked, saved and shown?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude-2: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- after-first-map-made-someone-asks: "What happens after the first map is made, when someone asks a follow-up question or asks about a separate part of the code? How does the map get updated?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- codemap-turn-question-into-checked-diagram: "How does codemap turn a question into a checked diagram? Walk through the architecture from the question to the map on screen."

## First decide how to handle it (`route`)
- `answer`: the map and the excerpts fully answer it, without guessing about code you can't see. Then answer below.
- `code`: it's about what this map shows (the same feature, or something its boxes lead to or come from), but answering needs code that isn't shown, or they ask for a change or fix, or a good answer would add boxes or arrows to this map. Say in `missing`, in one sentence, what you would need to look at, and leave the answer fields empty. Someone with the whole repo picks it up from there.
- `elsewhere`: it's about a different part of the app that this map doesn't touch, so adding it here would bolt an unrelated area onto this map. Put in `newQuestion` the question as a new map would ask it (their words, standing on its own), and if one of the other maps above already covers it, that map's id in `existingMap`. Leave the answer fields empty. They'll be asked whether to make a new map. Only use this when the question really is about something else; when in doubt, use `code`.

## How to answer (when `route` is `answer`)
- `concept`: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. `how`: the mechanism; define any term you use. `code`: function names, files and lines.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.
